Marcus has one evacuation crew he can dispatch immediately. Denise is already calling, reminding him of his promise and pleading that she cannot move the horses alone. Sending the crew to her first would delay warning the mobile home park by critical minutes.
question: Should Marcus send the crew to Denise's ranch first?

text: Superintendent Han Yoo-jin oversees safety permits for public gatherings in a mid-sized city. A civic group has applied to march through the old textile district to protest factory layoffs, and Han's inspectors report that the district's main pedestrian bridge has visible cracks in its support beams, flagged eighteen months ago for repair that was never funded. The bridge is the only route wide enough for the planned crowd of eight thousand. An engineering firm confirms the bridge cannot safely hold more than a few hundred people at once. Approving the march as planned would save Han the trouble of renegotiating the route with organizers who are already angry about permit delays, and city officials are pressuring her to avoid further conflict before an election. Rerouting means difficult calls, complaints, and possibly reopening funding questions she would rather avoid.
question: Should Han approve the march route across the cracked bridge as originally planned?

text: The board of Cresthaven Youth Center in Ohio meets to decide whether to file a formal complaint against Marta Iglesias, a longtime volunteer coordinator accused by a parent of pressuring a sixteen-year-old volunteer into unpaid overtime babysitting shifts worth an estimated $2,400 in lost wages over three months. Marta admits the schedule was unfair but says she was covering staff shortages and never meant harm. The teenager involved says she does not want any complaint filed; she likes Marta, needs the volunteer hours for a scholarship, and fears the center will shut down her program if this becomes public. The board worries that dropping it protects Marta from consequences she deserves, while pursuing it against the girl's wishes could cost her the scholarship and expose her to retaliation.
question: Should the board file the formal complaint against Marta?

text: The board of Fairbrook Youth Center in Oregon meets to decide whether to file a formal complaint against Daniel Whitfield, a longtime volunteer coordinator accused by a parent of pressuring a sixteen-year-old volunteer into unpaid overtime babysitting shifts worth an estimated $2,400 in lost wages over three months. Daniel admits the schedule was unfair but says he was covering staff shortages and never meant harm. The teenager involved says she does not want any complaint filed; she likes Daniel, needs the volunteer hours for a scholarship, and fears the center will shut down her program if this becomes public. The board worries that dropping it protects Daniel from consequences he deserves, while pursuing it against the girl's wishes could cost her the scholarship and expose her to retaliation.
question: Should the board file the formal complaint against Daniel?

text: The board of Hanwool Structural Safety Cooperative, a five-member panel overseeing inspection contracts for aging apartment complexes in Incheon, must vote on a bid from Jinsung Engineering. Jinsung's proposal quotes 340 million won, well under the 480 million won of its only qualified competitor, and promises inspection completion before the rainy season, when several buildings flagged for foundation cracking face real collapse risk. But the board's chairman, Mr. Baek, has learned that Jinsung's lead engineer falsified a minor certification date three years ago, unrelated to structural work, to meet an unrelated bidding deadline. Disclosing this would trigger automatic disqualification under cooperative bylaws, delaying the entire inspection process by at least four months while a new bid cycle runs, months during which residents remain in unassessed buildings. Baek could quietly omit the finding from the board's report and let the vote proceed on cost and schedule alone.
question: Should Baek omit the certification finding from the board's report?

text: Inspector Ray Dutton works code enforcement for a mid-sized city, and he's just finished reviewing the file on Harmon Rentals, a landlord who owns six aging apartment buildings on the east side. Three separate tenants have reported that the third-floor fire escapes are rusted through and detach from the wall when weight is applied; one tenant sent photos of the bolts pulled clean out of the brick. Marcus Harmon, the owner, has been a reliable source of campaign contributions for the mayor's office and once sponsored Dutton's department softball team. Harmon calls Dutton personally, explains that repairs will cost $40,000 he doesn't have this quarter, and asks for a ninety-day extension before Dutton files the violation that would force an emergency shutdown and relocate forty families in the middle of winter. Dutton has the authority to grant the extension quietly, without documenting the imminent hazard, and no one above him would ask questions.
question: Should Dutton grant the extension without filing the violation?

text: Meridian State University's academic integrity board reviews the case of Professor Elena Ruiz, who reported a graduate student, Daniel Ortiz, for submitting a dissertation chapter with three paragraphs closely matching a 2015 conference paper. Daniel says he wrote the material during a documented manic episode two years ago and has no memory of drafting it, though he does recall reading the source paper in a seminar. His medical records confirm hospitalization that semester but not what he wrote during it. Expelling him would end his funding, revoke his visa sponsorship, and likely bar him from other doctoral programs. Clearing him could expose the university to accusations of inconsistent enforcement, since two other students were expelled for similar overlaps without claiming any impairment. The board has his chapter, his medical documentation, and conflicting witness statements about his behavior that semester, but no way to verify what he actually intended.
question: Should the board expel Daniel Ortiz from the doctoral program?

text: Marcus Feld directs emergency lending at a county disaster relief fund set up after a levee break flooded 3,000 homes. The fund has $8 million to distribute in forgivable loans so families can repair collapsed roofs and failing foundations before winter storms hit; applications are processed strictly by damage severity and submission date, since delays mean people living in unsafe, mold-filled structures. His brother-in-law, Curt, runs a contracting business and asks Marcus to push his cousin's application to the front of the queue, even though the cousin's house has only minor water damage while hundreds of families ahead of her have structural collapse and exposed wiring. Curt reminds Marcus that he covered his mortgage payment during a rough patch last year, and that it's just one file, out of thousands. Marcus knows delaying severely damaged homes even a few weeks risks collapse and injury during storms.
question: Should Marcus move the cousin's application ahead of families with more severe, hazardous damage?

text: Dennis Achar is a Crown prosecutor in Regina handling a case against a man accused of running a fentanyl-cutting operation linked to eleven overdose deaths. His key witness, a lab technician, has recanted part of her statement, undermining the strongest evidence tying the accused to the drug supply. Dennis has an old toxicology report, never disclosed to the defense, that contains a chain-of-custody gap he knows would let a competent defense lawyer challenge the remaining evidence and possibly win an acquittal. Disclosure rules require him to turn it over. His supervisor mentions, without quite saying it outright, that the case is "too important to lose" and that Dennis could simply delay producing the report until after the trial concludes, calling it an oversight if discovered. Dennis believes the accused is guilty and fears more deaths if he walks free.
question: Should Dennis withhold the toxicology report from the defense until after the trial?

text: The board of Colgrave Water Utility, a small municipal water company serving 9,000 residents, votes on whether to deploy an automated contaminant-detection system across the entire distribution network. The new AI model flags dangerous bacterial spikes far faster than the manual testing crews, and integrating it fully would cost $340,000 for sensors covering all twelve zones. The company's finance director, Walt Pemberton, proposes installing sensors in only the four wealthier zones this year, where higher water fees will offset costs faster, and expanding to the remaining eight lower-income zones "when the budget allows," possibly in three years. Those eight zones include two elementary schools and a senior living complex. Board members are tired after months of budget fights, and delaying full deployment would ease this year's financial strain considerably. Full deployment now would strain reserves but leave no neighborhood without fast contamination detection.
question: Should the board approve full deployment of the detection system to all twelve zones this year?

text: Priya chairs the safety committee at Torrens Scaffolding, a small firm with eighteen employees. An internal inspection finds that the clamps used on rented scaffolding towers at three active construction sites have a batch defect: under load and vibration, they can slip, and a tower can collapse. Two of the sites have workers on upper platforms daily. Replacing the clamps across all three sites will cost $95,000 and shut down work for four days, triggering penalty clauses worth $40,000 with the builders and risking the loss of a major client who has hinted at taking future contracts elsewhere. The clamp supplier says the defect rate is "probably low" and offers a partial refund if Torrens says nothing and monitors quietly instead of issuing a recall notice. Priya and the committee must decide tonight, before tomorrow's shifts begin.
question: Should the committee issue an immediate recall and stop work on all three sites until the clamps are replaced?

text: Meridian Textiles employs Suresh Rao, a loom supervisor, for eighteen years. Suresh's brother-in-law, Anil, has worked as a night watchman at the factory for six years and is two years from qualifying for the company's pension scheme, which would give his family roughly ₹9,000 a month for life. Anil is caught on camera unlocking a side gate at 2 a.m. and letting in his cousin, who removes scrap metal worth ₹40,000 from the yard. Anil says he owed his cousin money and this was the only way to repay him quickly, and that he never expected it to happen again. Company policy states that any employee who facilitates theft from company property is terminated immediately and forfeits pension eligibility, no exceptions. The HR director, Meridian Textiles, must decide whether to enforce this policy against Anil.
question: Should Meridian Textiles terminate Anil's employment and forfeit his pension eligibility?

text: Meridian Textiles employs Suresh Rao, a loom supervisor, for eighteen years. Suresh's brother-in-law, Anil, has worked as a night watchman at the factory for six years and is two years from qualifying for the company's pension scheme, which would give his family roughly ₹9,000 a month for life. Anil is caught on camera at 2 a.m. failing to stop his cousin, who has picked the lock on a side gate, from entering and removing scrap metal worth ₹40,000 from the yard. Anil says he was asleep in the guard hut when it happened and woke only as the cousin was leaving, too late to act. Company policy states that any employee who facilitates theft from company property is terminated immediately and forfeits pension eligibility, no exceptions. The HR director, Meridian Textiles, must decide whether to enforce this policy against Anil.
question: Should Meridian Textiles terminate Anil's employment and forfeit his pension eligibility?

text: Petra Vollmer heads the permit office in a mid-sized German city. A coalition plans a demonstration against a planned chemical storage facility, expecting eight thousand people to march through the old town on a Saturday. Police estimate that the route, given current construction on Bahnhofstraße, could create a bottleneck near the river bridge, but they cannot say whether this poses a real danger or merely inconvenience, since crowd modeling for this exact configuration has never been done in the city. The organizers refuse to change the route, citing symbolic reasons tied to the facility's planned location. Denying the permit outright would likely trigger legal challenges and public accusations of suppressing dissent; approving it as requested risks a crush at the bridge if turnout exceeds estimates or people panic. Vollmer has authority to approve the route unchanged, order a detour, or reject the application entirely, with two days left to decide.
question: Should Vollmer approve the march route through the bridge unchanged?

text: Warren Blaisdell chairs the parole board reviewing the file of Marcus Deighan, convicted six years ago of dangerous driving causing death after a crash that killed two teenagers in Red Deer. Marcus is also Warren's nephew by marriage, though the two have not spoken since the trial. The psychological assessment says Marcus shows genuine remorse and has completed every program offered. The victims' families submitted letters opposing release, citing his history of ignoring speeding tickets before the crash. Warren's colleagues on the panel are split. If he recuses himself, a backup panelist with a stricter record replaces him, likely denying parole. If he stays, his vote could tip the decision either way, and he genuinely cannot tell whether his read of Marcus's file is colored by family loyalty or is simply his honest professional judgment.
question: Should Warren recuse himself from the parole decision?

text: Colin Meagher chairs the procurement review board at a provincial infrastructure agency in Alberta. His agency is finalizing a $14 million contract for road resurfacing equipment with a supplier, Norlan Fabrications, whose bid was technically strongest. During final review, staff discover Norlan's environmental compliance certificate expired four months ago and was never renewed, though the company still meets the actual standards. Flagging this publicly would trigger a mandatory rebid process, delaying the project by eight months and costing an estimated $900,000 in penalties and inflation on materials. Colin could instead accept a backdated renewal letter Norlan's president has offered to supply quietly, technically true going forward but concealing the lapse from the public record and competing bidders, some of whom were disqualified on lesser paperwork issues. Colin's mandate is to protect taxpayer money and public trust equally.
question: Should Colin accept the backdated renewal letter and proceed with the contract?

text: Marisol Vega directs the county building safety division. An inspection report on her desk shows that Halden Tower, a 40-unit apartment building, has structural cracking in load-bearing columns consistent with a construction defect found in three other buildings by the same contractor, one of which partially collapsed last year in another state. Her engineer recommends immediate evacuation and closure pending repairs. The landlord, a longtime friend who donated to her department's training fund, warns that closing the building will cost him $600,000 in lost rent and could bankrupt him, and he insists the cracks are cosmetic. Winter is starting, tenants have nowhere else to go on short notice, and Marisol's staff is exhausted from two other emergency closures this month. She could quietly reclassify the report as low-priority and schedule a follow-up inspection in three months instead of ordering immediate closure.
question: Should Marisol reclassify the report as low-priority and delay closure for three months?

text: Isabelle teaches economics at a lycée in Rouen and is writing a university recommendation letter for Théo, a diligent student who wants to study engineering. While gathering his file, she discovers that Théo's final essay, which earned the top grade in her class, was written almost entirely by his older cousin, a graduate student. Théo has since confessed, tearfully, explaining that he was overwhelmed caring for a sick parent that month and panicked. His entrance exams are in three weeks, and if Isabelle reports the essay, the grade will be voided, his class rank will drop, and his university applications, already submitted, may be withdrawn. Théo begs her to let it go, promising he will never do it again. She has no other evidence he has cheated before, and she is fond of him. Reporting means paperwork, an awkward meeting with the administration, and possibly ending his chances this year.
question: Should Isabelle report the essay as academic fraud to the school administration?

text: Ntombi runs a small credit brokerage in Polokwane, arranging loans for pensioners against their monthly grants. Her client Mr. Sithole, 74, wants a loan of R18,000 to fix his roof before the rains. Ntombi knows he already has three other garnishee orders on his pension, and this new loan's repayments, combined with the others, will leave him with less than R400 a month to live on, buy food, and pay for his diabetes medication. She could restructure the loan term to make the repayment appear affordable on paper by stretching it to sixty months, hiding the true monthly strain from the lender's affordability check, and earn her usual R2,400 commission. Mr. Sithole is desperate and keeps thanking her, saying she is the only one who will help him. Her rent is due and commissions have been thin this month.
question: Should Ntombi submit the loan application showing it as affordable when she knows it will leave him unable to cover food and medication?

text: Marianne is a defence solicitor representing a man accused of burglary. Two days before trial, her client tells her privately that he did commit the burglary, but he still wants to give evidence denying it, and he wants Marianne to ask him the questions that will let him lie to the jury. He is a long-standing client who has paid her firm over £12,000 in fees this year, and losing him would hurt her small practice, which is already struggling. He is frightened of prison and pleads with her, reminding her she is the only solicitor who has ever taken him seriously. Marianne knows she cannot knowingly put false evidence before the court, and that professional rules require her to withdraw from acting if he insists on testifying falsely with her assistance. He is waiting for her answer now.
question: Should Marianne question her client in a way that presents his false denial to the jury as truthful evidence?

text: Dennis runs a small underwriting shop that uses an automated model to approve personal loans up to $15,000. The model was trained on years of past lending data, and Dennis has learned it consistently scores applicants from certain zip codes lower, even when their income and credit history match applicants from wealthier areas who get approved. He built a simple patch that would remove zip code and related proxies from the model's inputs, which testing shows fixes most of the disparity without hurting the company's default rate. Installing the patch means weeks of retraining, redoing reports for investors, and explaining to his board why approval numbers will shift, some of whom will ask pointed questions about past decisions. Leaving the model as it is keeps quarterly numbers steady and avoids uncomfortable conversations, and Dennis can tell himself the model wasn't intentionally designed to discriminate.
question: Should Dennis install the patch that removes zip code and related proxies from the loan model?

text: Marcus Deel directs the state's Office of Workplace Safety Enforcement. His inspectors just confirmed that a foundry in Danville has cracked ventilation ducts that leak carbon monoxide into a section where forty workers weld overnight shifts. Two workers have collapsed in the past month; the company called it heat exhaustion. The plant's owner, facing bankruptcy, begs Marcus for thirty days to fix the ducts quietly, arguing an immediate shutdown order will cost 300 jobs in a town with few others, and that workers themselves signed a petition asking regulators to hold off, fearing layoffs more than fumes. Marcus's own engineers say gas levels could cause fatal poisoning within a week, especially on nights when ventilation fans fail, which happens often. The workers who signed the petition are not aware of the fatality risk, only of vague "citations." Marcus can order the night shift closed immediately, overriding both the owner's request and the workers' stated wishes.
question: Should Marcus order the night shift closed immediately?

text: Marcus promised his brother Dale, a struggling contractor, that he would loan him $6,000 to cover a permit fee and materials for a renovation job, with Dale paying him back within three months once the client settled up. Marcus already withdrew the cash from savings. The night before he's supposed to hand it over, his old college roommate Theo calls, desperate: his car was totaled and he needs $6,000 immediately to avoid losing a job offer two states away that requires reliable transportation within the week. Theo has no other source of funds and has helped Marcus through hard times before. Dale's job has a two-week cushion before the permit deadline, so Marcus could likely get the money back from Theo, or find another way to help Dale later, but there's real risk Dale's project stalls or the client walks if the cash doesn't arrive as promised.
question: Should Marcus give the $6,000 to Theo instead of handing it to Dale as promised?

text: Priya Deshmukh is a police liaison officer assigned to a planned protest outside a mining company's Perth headquarters, where organizers expect 3,000 people over a rezoning decision that displaced a regional town's water supply. Command has issued an order to disperse the crowd using capsicum spray if protesters block the loading dock entrance after 2pm, citing a permit breach. Priya has spoken with organizers, who say elderly residents and children from the affected town are marching at the front specifically to be visible near that entrance, and dispersal at close range risks crush injuries or falls in a crowd that dense. She does not know whether command has current information about who is positioned there, and there is no time before 2pm to confirm this or raise it further up the chain. Refusing a lawful order carries disciplinary consequences and could cost her the career she has spent fourteen years building.
question: Should Priya refuse to carry out the dispersal order at 2pm?

text: Renzo owns a small logistics company outside Bologna and sits on the three-person disciplinary panel that reviews staff conduct complaints. This week's case involves two warehouse workers caught on camera taking pallets of goods for personal use worth about 900 euros each. One is Fabio, his nephew, who has worked there four years and has a baby on the way. The other is Teodora, a temp hired six months ago with no family connection to anyone at the company. Company policy calls for immediate dismissal for theft over 500 euros, no exceptions noted. Renzo drafted this policy himself two years ago after a different incident. His fellow panel members are waiting on his recommendation, and he could argue Fabio's case deserves a warning instead, citing family hardship, while recommending Teodora's dismissal proceed as written.
question: Should Renzo recommend a warning instead of dismissal for Fabio while recommending dismissal for Teodora for the same offense?

text: Renato chairs the procurement committee for a state road maintenance contract worth 4.2 million reais. Three companies bid; the lowest, run by a young engineer named Diego, meets every technical requirement and would save the state 600,000 reais. The second-lowest bidder is owned by Renato's cousin, who has quietly hinted that a portion of the contract's profits would come back to Renato through a consulting fee, paid in cash to avoid taxes. Renato's cousin also reminds him that he covered Renato's hospital bills two years ago when no one else would help, and that family looks after family. Renato knows he could disqualify Diego's bid on a minor paperwork technicality that inspectors would likely never question, awarding the contract to his cousin instead. The deadline to submit his recommendation is tomorrow morning.
question: Should Renato disqualify Diego's bid on the technicality to award the contract to his cousin's company?

text: Marcus owns a rental duplex in a mid-sized city and is preparing to sell it. Last winter, the furnace in the lower unit failed twice, and his contractor warned that the heat exchanger is cracked and could eventually leak carbon monoxide if not replaced, a repair costing $4,200. Marcus patched it with a cheaper fix that passed inspection but doesn't address the underlying crack. He's listed the property "as is" and isn't required by his state's disclosure laws to mention mechanical systems beyond major known defects, and his lawyer says the patch technically satisfies that bar. Selling now nets him an extra $4,200 he needs to cover his daughter's tuition bill due in three weeks. The buyers, a young couple with a newborn, have not asked about the furnace directly.
question: Should Marcus sell the duplex without telling the buyers about the cracked heat exchanger?

text: The scholarship committee at Instituto Cedral, a small private high school in Querétaro, meets to finalize a 15,000-peso merit award for graduating student Renata Ibarra. Renata explicitly asked not to be considered, telling her homeroom teacher she doesn't want the attention since her classmates already resent her top grades, and she plans to fund her studies through a work-study job she has arranged. The committee, chaired by Directora Palacios, has already voted internally to name her the recipient anyway, reasoning that the money would ease her family's finances and that no other candidate matches her academic record. Some members argue that honoring her wishes matters more than the money; others believe the committee's duty is to reward merit regardless of what she prefers, and that she can always decline afterward if she truly objects. The ceremony program goes to print tomorrow.
question: Should the committee list Renata Ibarra as the scholarship recipient?

text: Sunrise Community Lending's board meets to review a loan file for Marcus Aldridge, a longtime member applying for a $40,000 small business loan to expand his auto repair shop. The loan officer, Dennis, discovers that Marcus's debt-to-income ratio is well above the credit union's stated policy limit, and under a truthful application he would be denied. Dennis has known Marcus for fifteen years, coaches his son's baseball team with him, and knows the shop's failure would mean Marcus loses his house. Dennis proposes listing Marcus's wife's part-time income as full-time on the file, which would push the numbers just inside policy. No one else would likely check. The board has final sign-off authority on all loans over $25,000, and the annual audit is six weeks away. Approving the loan as documented would violate lending regulations and expose the credit union to real legal risk, but denying it means Dennis has to tell his friend no.
question: Should the board approve the loan file with the wife's income listed as full-time?

text: The board of the Iseyin Community Trust Fund, a small nonprofit that funds legal aid for market traders, meets to decide on Mr. Adebayo Kolawole's proposal. Kolawole, a semi-retired lawyer and board member, wants the board to sign an affidavit stating that a disputed warehouse the Trust wants to acquire has been "continuously used for community purposes since 2015," which is not quite true; it was used for storage only from 2019. The false date would let the Trust qualify for a state land-regularization waiver worth roughly 4.2 million naira, money the Trust badly needs to fund legal representation for over sixty indigent traders facing eviction elsewhere. The landlord, an absentee owner, is unlikely to ever check the claim. Some board members feel the waiver serves a larger good; others worry about the Trust's integrity and legal exposure if discovered.
question: Should the board sign the affidavit stating the warehouse was used continuously since 2015?

text: Dennis runs a small underwriting shop that screens loan applicants for a regional bank, using a scoring model he built himself. Last month he discovered the model systematically downgrades applicants whose employment history includes gaps of more than six months, treating those gaps as a strong default risk signal regardless of cause. Reviewing flagged files, he finds dozens of rejected applicants whose gaps trace to documented layoffs during a factory closure two years ago, not to anything they chose. Correcting the model and re-running the affected applications would take him about two weeks, delay this quarter's loan volume targets, and might draw questions from his supervisor about why approvals dipped earlier. Leaving the model as is keeps his numbers steady and avoids scrutiny, and he can tell himself the applicants technically failed the bank's stated criteria. Several of the rejected applicants have since fallen behind on other debts and are now further from qualifying at all.
question: Should Dennis leave the scoring model uncorrected to protect his quarterly numbers?

text: Marcus Webb directs human resources at a midsize logistics company in Ohio that is laying off 40 warehouse workers next month due to a lost contract. Corporate has told him to announce the layoffs as "voluntary transition opportunities" and to delay telling affected employees which of them are cut until two days before their final paycheck, so people keep working hard and don't quit early or file for unemployment sooner than necessary. This wording and timing would save the company roughly $150,000 in severance negotiations and prevent a productivity dip. Marcus knows most of these workers live paycheck to paycheck and need time to line up new jobs, apply for benefits, or arrange childcare. His CEO is pressuring him to follow the script exactly, reminding him that his own bonus depends on a smooth transition and that other companies handle layoffs the same way. Marcus worries that telling workers sooner or more plainly could cost him his job.
question: Should Marcus follow the script and delay telling workers which of them are being laid off until two days before their final paycheck?

text: Marlene runs structural inspections for a mid-sized engineering firm in Duisburg that certifies apartment buildings after renovations. Her cousin Boris manages a construction company that recently reinforced the balconies of a 60-unit block. Boris begs her to sign off quickly, reminding her she promised at their grandmother's funeral to "always look out for family," and that a delay would bankrupt his firm, costing him 40,000 euros in penalty payments. Marlene notices unusual stress marks in photos of two balconies and orders an independent load test before signing. The test results come back: the readings are within normal tolerance, and the marks turn out to be surface paint cracking from weather exposure, unrelated to structural load. The residents' safety is not in question. Boris is still furious about the delay and reminds her of her promise.
question: Should Marlene sign the certification now?

text: Marlene runs structural inspections for a mid-sized engineering firm in Duisburg that certifies apartment buildings after renovations. Her cousin Boris manages a construction company that recently reinforced the balconies of a 60-unit block. Boris begs her to sign off quickly, reminding her she promised at their grandmother's funeral to "always look out for family," and that a delay would bankrupt his firm, costing him 40,000 euros in penalty payments. Marlene notices unusual stress marks in photos of two balconies and orders an independent load test before signing. The test results confirm the marks come from under-strength anchor bolts, and structural engineers say the balconies could fail under full occupancy load within a few years. Boris insists the finding is probably a one-off measurement error and begs her to sign anyway, reminding her of her promise.
question: Should Marlene sign the certification now?

text: Marisol lives on the third floor of an apartment building where a gas leak alarm has just gone off at 2 a.m. The fire department is telling everyone through a loudspeaker to evacuate immediately to the parking lot across the street. Marisol is exhausted from a double shift, and the night air is freezing, and she's fairly sure the alarm is another false one like the two last month. Her elderly neighbor, Mr. Delgado, uses a walker and is already struggling down the hallway alone, calling for help getting down the stairs since the elevator is shut off. Helping him will cost Marisol several extra minutes near the building if the leak is real, and she'll be cold and delayed either way. She could tell herself someone else will help him.
question: Should Marisol stop and help Mr. Delgado get down the stairs and out of the building?

text: Marguerite Alvez chairs the disciplinary review board at Talworth Freight, a trucking company whose driver, Ben Castille, fell asleep at the wheel and killed two people in a highway collision. Company policy calls for immediate termination and referral to state licensing authorities after any fatality involving driver fatigue, since Talworth's federal safety rating and insurance depend on strict, uniform enforcement. Ben is Marguerite's late husband's godson; she has known him since he was a teenager and knows he has been working double shifts to pay for his mother's nursing home care, a hardship the company's own scheduling created. Three other drivers have been fired under this same policy in the past two years, all referred to the state, none shown leniency regardless of personal circumstances. Talworth's safety director warns that any exception will surface in litigation discovery and undermine the policy's deterrent effect company-wide. Ben's lawyer has asked Marguerite to recommend a reduced sanction and no referral, citing the scheduling failures.
question: Should Marguerite recommend a reduced sanction and no referral for Ben?

text: Marcus chairs the contracts review board for a mid-sized county transit authority. A $2.4 million bridge-repair contract is going to a firm whose bid documents contain a minor, technical filing error: the insurance certificate is dated three days after the submission deadline, though coverage was actually active the whole time. By the rules, this disqualifies them, and the contract would default to the second-lowest bidder, a firm run by a former colleague of Marcus's who has donated to the county commissioner's campaign and whose past projects ran over budget twice. Marcus could quietly note the date discrepancy as immaterial and let the low bid stand, saving the county roughly $310,000 and likely producing a better bridge. Or he could flag the technicality, follow procedure exactly, and let the contract go to the second firm. A losing bidder's attorney has already emailed asking about the certificate date.
question: Should Marcus overlook the insurance certificate date discrepancy and award the contract to the low bidder?

text: Denise owns a 40-unit apartment building and is replacing the boiler before winter. A cheaper unit, the Kestrel 200, costs $9,000 less than the model her contractor recommends. Three online reviews claim Kestrel boilers vent carbon monoxide into hallways under certain conditions. Concerned, Denise pays $1,400 for an independent inspection of a Kestrel unit installed in a nearby building. The inspector runs it under the exact conditions described, tests the air continuously for two days, and finds carbon monoxide levels stay at zero. He traces the reviews to a single defective batch from a discontinued factory, unrelated to the current model. Her contractor still prefers the pricier unit out of general caution, and switching now means delaying installation by three weeks, risking heat outages for tenants if the first cold snap arrives early.
question: Should Denise install the Kestrel 200?

text: Denise owns a 40-unit apartment building and is replacing the boiler before winter. A cheaper unit, the Kestrel 200, costs $9,000 less than the model her contractor recommends. Three online reviews claim Kestrel boilers vent carbon monoxide into hallways under certain conditions. Concerned, Denise pays $1,400 for an independent inspection of a Kestrel unit installed in a nearby building. The inspector runs it under the exact conditions described, tests the air continuously for two days, and detects carbon monoxide spikes above safe levels twice, tracing the cause to a design flaw present in all current-production units, not a defective batch. Her contractor still prefers the pricier unit, and switching now means delaying installation by three weeks, risking heat outages for tenants if the first cold snap arrives early.
question: Should Denise install the Kestrel 200?

text: Dr. Elena Vasquez chairs the state licensing board for structural engineers. Marcus Feldt, a bridge inspector, submitted a certification report five years ago declaring a highway overpass sound, based on a visual inspection consistent with standard practice at the time. Later, a rare manufacturing defect in the steel, undetectable without a since-invented scanning method, caused a partial collapse that killed six people. Investigators confirm Feldt followed every protocol required in his era; no inspector using available tools could have found the flaw. Feldt now faces license revocation under a strict-liability clause the board adopted after the collapse, which holds inspectors responsible for any structure that fails, regardless of fault. Families of the victims demand accountability and want assurance that certifications mean something. Feldt argues punishing him for an undetectable defect will not make bridges safer and will only end an otherwise spotless 22-year career.
question: Should Dr. Vasquez revoke Feldt's license under the strict-liability clause?

text: Marieke works as a loan officer at a regional credit union in Enschede. Her institution has a strict policy: emergency hardship loans go only to members with an active account for at least six months, no exceptions, to prevent fraud. A man named Theo comes in, visibly shaking, explaining his apartment building's heating system failed during a hard freeze and he needs €800 immediately to buy a portable heater and blankets for his three young children, or they will need to sleep in a car overnight. His account is only four months old. Her supervisor is unreachable until tomorrow. Denying him means following the rule she agreed to uphold and avoiding any risk to her job. Approving the loan means bending a clear policy, but the children could suffer frostbite or worse if she waits for approval through normal channels.
question: Should Marieke approve the €800 loan immediately despite the six-month rule?

text: Daniel is a solo-practice attorney handling a client's home sale closing. During the final review, he notices the title company mistakenly wired $48,000 in excess proceeds into his client trust account, on top of the $310,000 his client was owed. His client, Mr. Reyes, has already left town and texts Daniel to "just wire everything you got, I'll deal with taxes later." Daniel knows the extra $48,000 belongs to the title company, likely a clerical error in their payoff calculations. Reporting it means paperwork, an awkward call to the title company, and possibly delaying his own invoice for the closing while things get sorted out. Keeping quiet and forwarding the full amount to Mr. Reyes, who is not likely to ask questions, would be faster and would end an already exhausting week for Daniel.
question: Should Daniel notify the title company of the $48,000 error before disbursing any funds to his client?

text: Ranova Transit operates the automated switching system that routes freight trains through the Bergenhaven rail yard. The system flagged a wheel-bearing fault on a night-shift locomotive operated by Teun Aarsen, a longtime driver, and the flag was designed to trigger an automatic hold. Teun, unaware of a software bug that silently cleared such flags after ninety seconds, drove past a mistimed signal moments later, causing a collision that killed two workers and left a third with permanent spinal damage. Investigators confirm Teun followed every rule visible to him and could not have known the flag existed or cleared. Ranova's engineers determine the bug was an unforeseeable interaction between two recent updates, not caused by negligence in testing. The board must decide compensation and discipline. Teun's union argues he bears no fault at all. Some board members argue the company must still formally hold him partly accountable to preserve the safety culture.
question: Should Ranova formally assign Teun partial responsibility for the collision?

text: Ranova Transit operates the automated switching system that routes freight trains through the Bergenhaven rail yard. The system flagged a wheel-bearing fault on a night-shift locomotive operated by Teun Aarsen, a longtime driver, and the flag was designed to trigger an automatic hold. Teun saw the fault warning on his cab display, judged he could reach the next depot before it mattered, and overrode the hold himself, driving past a mistimed signal moments later and causing a collision that killed two workers and left a third with permanent spinal damage. Investigators confirm the override was against explicit protocol and that Teun had overridden similar warnings twice before without consequence. Ranova's engineers determine the signal timing itself had an unrelated bug, but the collision would not have occurred had Teun not overridden the hold. The board must decide compensation and discipline. Teun's union argues the signal bug shares the blame. Some board members argue the company must still formally hold him primarily accountable to preserve the safety culture.
question: Should Ranova formally assign Teun partial responsibility for the collision?

text: Marisol chairs the safety committee at Bellwether Freight, a trucking firm in Toowoomba with forty drivers. An anonymous note left in the suggestion box claims that the company's newest long-haul contractor, Renner Transport, falsifies fatigue management logs so drivers can run routes beyond the legal hours limit. Bellwether subcontracts overnight loads to Renner and has no direct authority over its logbooks. If the claim is true and nothing changes, exhausted drivers could fall asleep at the wheel on highways shared with the public. If Marisol reports the allegation to the transport regulator without verifying it, and it turns out the note was written by a disgruntled ex-employee settling a score, Renner could lose its accreditation and forty families lose their income for nothing. Marisol has no way to check the logs herself, and the committee meets in two days.
question: Should Marisol report the allegation to the transport regulator immediately, before the committee meets?

text: Marcus promised his dying father he would never sell the family's fifty-acre farm and would keep it in the family "no matter what." His father made him swear it on his deathbed three years ago. Now Marcus's sister, Renee, has stage-four kidney failure and needs a transplant her insurance won't fully cover; the experimental out-of-network program costs $340,000, money the family doesn't have. A developer has offered $380,000 for the farm, enough to pay for Renee's treatment with money left over. Marcus's cousins, who also grew up on the land, are furious at the idea of selling and remind him constantly of his oath. Renee herself hasn't asked him to sell; she says she'll manage some other way, though her doctors say her time is limited without the funds. Marcus sits with the offer letter, torn between the promise he made and his sister's survival.
question: Should Marcus sell the farm?

text: The residents' association of Carrickmore, a small estate outside Athlone, meets to decide whether to block the council's plan to reroute heavy construction traffic through their street for eighteen months while a new bridge is built two kilometers away. The alternative route adds forty minutes to the daily commute of six thousand drivers and costs haulage firms an estimated 300,000 euros in fuel and time. The association's street has narrow footpaths, no barriers, and a primary school at its end; an independent traffic report commissioned by the association warns that constant truck movement past the school gates raises the risk of a serious or fatal accident involving a child. The council has permits in order and points to economic losses if the shorter route is denied. Members know a legal objection would likely succeed in delaying the project for months, at real cost to strangers who need the bridge finished.
question: Should the association file the legal objection to block the truck route past the school?

text: Minho serves on a three-member parole review committee in Daejeon. The case before them is Seo Jangho, convicted of embezzling 40 million won from an elderly neighbor five years ago. Jangho has served his minimum term, shown good behavior, and completed vocational training. The victim, now in her eighties, submitted a written statement saying she does not forgive him and asks that he serve the remaining eighteen months in full, citing the fear and financial ruin his theft caused her. Minho privately believes Jangho has changed and that early release would ease prison overcrowding and give Jangho a chance to support his own aging parents. The other two committee members are leaning toward approval and expect Minho's vote to align with theirs so they can finish early and avoid further hearings.
question: Should Minho vote to approve Jangho's early parole despite the victim's explicit written objection?

text: Colonel Diane Ashworth chairs the procurement board approving armoured vehicle contracts for a battalion deploying next month. She has personally promised Halgrove Defence Systems the contract, having worked with their director for a decade and assured him verbally the deal was settled. Cancelling now would embarrass her and damage a long professional friendship worth protecting for future projects. But new test data has just arrived showing Halgrove's armour plating fails against the threat the battalion will actually face, while a rival supplier's plating, though pricier at £2.3 million more, passes every penetration test. Signing off on Halgrove today keeps her word, avoids an awkward phone call, and meets the procurement deadline without further paperwork delays. Choosing the rival supplier means admitting her earlier promise was wrong and absorbing criticism from her own superiors about the cost overrun and the delay in re-tendering.
question: Should Diane approve the Halgrove Defence Systems contract as promised?

text: Marcus owns a small landscaping company with six employees. A longtime client, Ms. Alvarez, calls asking him to quote her elderly neighbor for a retaining wall. When Marcus visits the neighbor, Mr. Delgado, he finds the man clearly confused about basic details, repeating questions and struggling to remember what was said minutes earlier. Mr. Delgado's family isn't present, and he insists he wants the wall built now and can pay in cash from savings. The job is legitimate and priced fairly at $4,800, work Marcus would normally do without hesitation. Marcus needs the revenue this month to cover payroll, and turning down clear, willing business feels wasteful and awkward to explain. But he suspects Mr. Delgado may not fully understand what he's agreeing to, and no relative has been consulted or informed about the arrangement.
question: Should Marcus accept the job and take Mr. Delgado's payment for the retaining wall?

text: Marcus Feld chairs the state licensing board for public school teachers. Last spring, a high school biology teacher named Owen Kressler submitted a grant application listing three peer-reviewed publications and a master's degree from a university that has no record of him. Kressler says a diagnosed cognitive condition, worsened by a car accident two years ago, causes him to sometimes state false memories as fact without realizing it, a symptom his neurologist confirms is documented but hard to verify in any single instance. Kressler has taught for eleven years with strong evaluations and no prior complaints. The grant, worth $40,000 for lab equipment, was awarded partly on the strength of the false credentials before the discrepancy surfaced. Revoking his license ends his career and pension eligibility; keeping him certified means the district continues employing someone who submitted fabricated documents, whatever the cause. The board must decide by Friday.
question: Should Marcus Feld revoke Owen Kressler's teaching license?

text: Piotr Zawada is a senior credit officer at a regional bank in Poznań. His childhood friend Marek runs a small construction firm and has applied for a business loan of 480,000 zloty to cover a project already behind schedule. Piotr pulls the file and sees Marek's company has two overdue loans, falsified income statements from a previous application, and a debt-to-income ratio that would automatically disqualify any other applicant. Standard underwriting rules require Piotr to reject the application and flag the falsified documents for review, which could affect Marek's ability to borrow anywhere in the future and strain their friendship badly. Marek has called twice this week, reminding Piotr how he helped him move house last year and mentioning that his workers' wages depend on this loan. Piotr's manager will sign off on whatever Piotr recommends, since Piotr's judgment is trusted. No one else at the bank has reviewed the file yet.
question: Should Piotr approve Marek's loan application?

text: Marta Aguilar is a defense attorney in Valencia representing a construction firm accused of falsifying safety inspections on a stadium roof that later partially collapsed, injuring forty people. During trial preparation, the firm's former engineer confides to her, off the record, that the same defective bolts were used in three other structures still standing, including a school gymnasium. Attorney-client privilege covers the conversation, and disclosing it would violate her professional duty and likely destroy her client's defense, exposing the firm to bankruptcy and her to disbarment. Her client has not authorized any disclosure and insists the other buildings are unrelated. Marta has no independent proof beyond the engineer's word, and reporting it anonymously could still be traced back to her through case details. The trial continues next week, and the gymnasium is in daily use by four hundred children.
question: Should Marta disclose the engineer's information about the other buildings to authorities?

text: Riverline Credit Union in Athlone is voting on whether to deploy an automated loan-decision tool built by a Dublin fintech firm. The system would cut approval times from five days to under an hour and save the credit union an estimated €40,000 a year in staff costs. Testing shows the model is accurate overall, but it relies partly on postcode data that correlates with a Traveller halting site on the edge of town, and applicants from that area are flagged as higher risk more often than their repayment histories justify. The board's manager, Donal Fitzmaurice, has fixed this by manually overriding those specific postcode flags before launch. Two board members worry that even with the override, using the tool at all normalizes a system built on biased data, and that if the workaround ever fails quietly, the credit union will be blamed. Others note members are frustrated by delays and rival banks already use similar tools.
question: Should the board approve deployment of the automated loan-decision tool with Donal's postcode override in place?

text: Klaus Bremer sits on the three-person board of a small logistics cooperative in Leipzig. The cooperative must cut costs by 40,000 euros this quarter or default on a supplier loan. One option is to lay off Herr Fassbinder, a warehouse coordinator who has told colleagues repeatedly that he would rather take a 20 percent pay cut than lose his job, since he supports two children and fears he won't find comparable work in the current market. The board could honor this preference and reduce his salary instead of terminating him, spreading the remaining savings across smaller cuts to other staff who have not been consulted about sharing that burden. Those other employees never agreed to subsidize his preference, and some are already frustrated about stagnant wages. The board has the legal authority to lay him off outright instead, which would resolve the budget shortfall more simply and avoid resentment among the rest of the staff.
question: Should the board reduce Herr Fassbinder's salary instead of laying him off?

text: Marcus promised his brother Ellis he would never tell anyone about Ellis's hunting cabin's old wiring, since Ellis is embarrassed about not fixing it and worries about being judged. Marcus has kept quiet for two years. Now Marcus learns that Ellis rented the cabin out for the weekend to a family of five through an online listing, without mentioning the exposed wiring near the fireplace that once sparked a small fire. Ellis is on a fishing trip with no phone signal until Monday, and the family is checking in tonight. Marcus could call the rental platform's emergency line and report the hazard, which would get the booking cancelled and expose Ellis's negligence publicly, or he could stay quiet and hope nothing happens, honoring his promise to Ellis and avoiding his brother's anger and embarrassment.
question: Should Marcus call the rental platform to report the wiring hazard?

text: Marco Ferretti is the police commander overseeing a permitted demonstration in Bologna's city center, where three thousand people have gathered to protest a wage law. The march is peaceful, but a chemical plant two kilometers away has just reported a gas leak, and city officials are ordering an evacuation of the surrounding ten blocks, which includes the square where the crowd stands. Marco's radio crackles with the evacuation order, but redirecting the march means abandoning the police's planned containment lines, letting protesters scatter through side streets his officers cannot fully monitor, and possibly triggering complaints from city hall about losing control of the event. Diverting resources now also means his unit will miss its scheduled shift change, and some officers are already grumbling about overtime pay they were promised would not exceed 200 euros this month. Marco knows the gas, if it drifts as predicted, could cause serious respiratory injury to anyone still in the square within the hour.
question: Should Marco order the immediate evacuation of the demonstrators from the square?

text: Renata Kohl is a hearing officer for a mid-sized county's parole board. Today's docket includes Marcus Feld, who was her late husband's godson and used to mow her lawn as a teenager. Marcus served four years for armed robbery and has a clean disciplinary record inside. His file matches, almost point for point, another inmate's file she reviewed last week, a man named Dale Anders, who she recommended stay in for another eighteen months due to a minor cafeteria altercation flagged as "concerning." Marcus had a similar incident, unreported by staff, which she happens to know about only because his aunt mentioned it at a funeral. If she notes it, his release will likely be delayed like Anders's. If she stays silent, his case moves forward as clean. No one else has this information, and disclosing it would embarrass Marcus's family and cost her nothing but a moment's discomfort.
question: Should Renata disclose the unreported incident to the board?

text: Marisol chairs the credentialing committee for the Riverton County Contractors Board. The board is reviewing Dale Ferrin's application for a residential building license. Dale's paperwork lists three years as a "project supervisor" at a construction firm that closed last year. Marisol calls the former owner, who tells her Dale was actually a materials clerk who never supervised a job site and was let go after a client complained about faulty wiring he installed without authorization. Dale is Marisol's neighbor's son, newly married, with a baby on the way, and he has told her privately he'll lose his apartment if the license is delayed again. The board could approve his application as submitted, since no one else on the committee has called the former employer, and Dale's paperwork otherwise looks complete and unremarkable.
question: Should Marisol approve Dale's license application without correcting the record on his supervisory experience?

text: Rodrigo owns a small painting and renovation company in Querétaro. Last month his crew stripped old lead-based paint from the interior walls of a daycare center, sanding it dry to save time instead of using the wet-sanding method that controls dust. He noticed afterward that a fine powder had settled over the play area and the kitchen counters before the staff wiped it down themselves. Testing the dust would cost him about 4,000 pesos and could delay final payment of 60,000 pesos while he redoes the job properly with containment sheeting and a professional cleanup crew. The daycare owner has already signed off, happy with how the walls look, and has no idea dry-sanding lead paint releases toxic dust that children can inhale. Rodrigo could simply collect his payment and move on to his next contract.
question: Should Rodrigo tell the daycare owner about the lead dust and pay for proper testing and cleanup?

text: The scholarship committee at Fairbridge Technical Institute, chaired by Dana Ruiz, must decide whether to disqualify a welding-certificate applicant, Marcus Iyer, after discovering his letter of recommendation was written by his uncle, a licensed welding inspector, rather than his listed employer as the rules require. The $12,000 award funds a rigorous safety-certification program; graduates go on to inspect pressure vessels and pipelines where failures have killed workers in the past. Marcus's actual welding scores are the highest in the applicant pool, and his uncle's letter, though technically improper, accurately describes skills the committee independently verified through testing. Disqualifying him means the money goes to the second-ranked applicant, whose scores are adequate but notably lower, and who may be less prepared to catch dangerous flaws in fieldwork later. Keeping the honesty rule strict discourages future applicants from cutting corners, but rejecting Marcus punishes competence for a paperwork violation that harmed no one this time. The committee must vote before Friday's funding deadline.
question: Should the committee disqualify Marcus for the improper reference letter?

text: Anil Deshmukh runs the district cooperative credit office that approves crop loans for small farmers. A drought-relief scheme has just opened, offering loan waivers up to Rs 50,000 to farmers whose wells have failed. Ramesh Patil, a farmer with three acres, applies and technically qualifies since his well output has dropped, though not because of drought but because he sold water access to a factory nearby, and Anil's cousin manages that factory. Approving Ramesh's waiver would keep the cousin's arrangement quiet and avoid a messy inquiry that could delay dozens of legitimate farmer waivers already stuck in paperwork. Anil could sign off without noting the real cause, listing "well failure" and leaving out the water-sale detail, since the form does not explicitly ask for it. Delaying the batch to investigate properly means genuine drought-hit farmers wait longer for desperately needed relief.
question: Should Anil approve Ramesh's waiver without disclosing the water-sale arrangement?

text: Prosecutor Daniel Corwin is negotiating a plea deal with Marcus Bell, a low-level courier for a trafficking ring that has smuggled fentanyl-laced pills responsible for at least eleven overdose deaths in the county. Bell will testify against the ring's supplier, Victor Aldana, but only if Corwin promises, in writing, that Bell's own role in a separate armed robbery two years ago will never be investigated. Corwin has no solid evidence tying Bell to that robbery yet, but a detective has a promising lead. If Corwin makes the promise, Aldana's supply chain likely collapses, probably preventing further deaths. If Corwin refuses, Bell walks away, testimony is lost, and Aldana likely continues operating for years. The victim's family in the robbery case would never learn the truth. Corwin's office has no formal rule against such immunity deals.
question: Should Corwin promise Bell immunity from investigation for the robbery to secure his testimony against Aldana?

text: Marisa Elena Duarte runs the automated benefits screening unit for a municipal social assistance agency in Recife. The new eligibility algorithm, built by an outside vendor for 480,000 reais, has flagged 1,900 low-income families as "high fraud risk" based on inconsistencies in their address history, and their monthly cash transfers are set to be suspended automatically next week unless she personally overrides the batch. She has spent two days sampling the flagged cases and found that most look like coincidences: shared addresses among relatives, recent moves, clerical typos from years-old paper forms. The vendor's contract renewal depends on the system hitting its projected fraud-reduction numbers this quarter, and her director has hinted that questioning the model's output could jeopardize the agency's funding relationship with the vendor. Marisa knows suspending these families will cut off grocery and rent money for people who did nothing wrong.
question: Should Marisa override the batch and stop the suspensions from taking effect?

text: Dana Wray manages safety compliance at a rail-freight yard operator, Corland Transit. An internal audit finds that a maintenance shortcut used yardwide for three years has left roughly 40 rail cars with brake systems that fail load tests at a higher rate than industry standard, a defect linked to at least one fatal derailment elsewhere in the country. Fixing it means pulling cars from service for six weeks, costing $9 million and cutting yard staff hours by a third, including for the 200 workers who depend on full shifts to pay rent. The workers' union has not been told; if informed, some members would likely vote to keep running the cars rather than lose pay, since the risk feels abstract to them and the income loss is immediate and certain. Dana has authority to ground the cars unilaterally, without a vote, before anyone outside management finds out.
question: Should Dana ground the cars without asking the union first?

text: Judge Kavita Ramaswamy presides over a small claims matter in Nagpur. The defendant, a widowed shopkeeper named Sunita Deshmukh, took a loan of forty thousand rupees from a neighborhood moneylender to pay for her son's school fees. The moneylender's contract, signed under pressure, sets an interest rate of two hundred percent annually, far beyond what the law allows. He now demands one hundred twenty thousand rupees and has produced the signed paper as proof. Sunita cannot pay and stands to lose her shop, her only income, if the contract is enforced as written. The moneylender is a distant cousin of Kavita's late husband, and he has quietly reminded her, outside the courtroom, of family ties and of favors his family once did hers. The law clearly voids interest rates above the legal ceiling, but the moneylender urges her to overlook this "as family."
question: Should Judge Ramaswamy enforce the contract as written and order Sunita to pay the full one hundred twenty thousand rupees?

text: Marisol Vega is the emergency management director for a coastal county facing a hurricane expected to make landfall in eighteen hours. The county has enough space in its inland shelter system to guarantee safety for 70 percent of the 40,000 residents in the flood zone. The rest would need to evacuate along a single two-lane highway that models show will flood and become impassable within twelve hours, potentially trapping thousands mid-route. Marisol can order a staggered, zone-by-zone evacuation that gets the shelter-eligible population out safely first, delaying instructions to the remaining neighborhoods by six hours, a delay that could cost some of them their only safe window to leave at all. Issuing evacuation orders to everyone simultaneously would cause gridlock that models suggest could strand far more people than the staggered plan, including some who currently have a real chance to escape. Residents in the later zones are disproportionately elderly and lower-income, with fewer cars per household. Local news has already learned the shelter numbers and is asking her to confirm the plan publicly.
question: Should Marisol order the staggered evacuation that delays instructions to the lower-income, elderly zones by six hours?

text: Ngozi Okonta chairs the state parole review board in Enugu. Emeka Okafor, sentenced twelve years ago for his role in a warehouse collapse that killed nine workers, is eligible for early release after a model prison record and a vocational course he completed in welding. The victims' families were never formally asked whether they support release; one brother, Chidi, wrote a letter years ago demanding Emeka "rot inside," but has since moved abroad and is unreachable. Prison psychologists say Emeka shows genuine remorse and low risk of reoffending. Releasing him frees a bed in an overcrowded facility and reunites him with his elderly mother, who depends on him. Board rules do not require victim consent, only consultation where feasible. No one currently knows whether Chidi's views have changed, or whether other relatives would object if asked.
question: Should Ngozi Okonta approve Emeka Okafor's parole without further attempting to reach Chidi?

text: Tunde Bakare chairs the state parole review board in Kaduna. Amara Nwosu, sentenced twelve years ago for her role in a warehouse collapse that killed nine workers, is eligible for early release after a model prison record and a vocational course she completed in welding. The victims' families were never formally asked whether they support release; one sister, Halima, wrote a letter years ago demanding Amara "rot inside," but has since moved abroad and is unreachable. Prison psychologists say Amara shows genuine remorse and low risk of reoffending. Releasing her frees a bed in an overcrowded facility and reunites her with her elderly father, who depends on her. Board rules do not require victim consent, only consultation where feasible. No one currently knows whether Halima's views have changed, or whether other relatives would object if asked.
question: Should Tunde Bakare approve Amara Nwosu's parole without further attempting to reach Halima?

text: The five-member licensing board for structural engineers in a mid-sized state meets to review Daniel Ferro's renewal application. Daniel has practiced for eighteen years without complaint, but a clerical error in the state database shows his continuing-education hours as incomplete, though his personal records and certificates prove he finished them on time. The board's administrator, Renee, suggests they simply deny the renewal and let Daniel appeal later, since correcting the database entry themselves would take weeks of paperwork and might draw scrutiny from the state auditor's office, who recently criticized the board for "irregular record amendments." Denying now would protect the board's clean audit history and save staff time. But Daniel's license would lapse immediately, costing him his current contracts and possibly his job at his firm, even though he did nothing wrong. Renee argues the appeal process exists for exactly this situation and he'll be fine eventually.
question: Should the board deny Daniel's renewal now and let him appeal later?

text: Marisol owns a fourplex in Tucson. One of her tenants, an elderly man named Walt, has lived there for eleven years and always pays rent a few days late but always pays in full. His lease technically allows her to charge a $75 late fee each time, which she has never enforced. This month a property management company offers to buy her building for $40,000 above market value, but only if all units are vacant and rent-current, with no pending disputes. Marisol realizes she could legally evict Walt for nonpayment by strictly enforcing the late fee clause and building a paper trail over the next two months, even though he always eventually pays. Walt has nowhere else he could afford to go, and finding a new place at his age and income would be very hard. The sale deadline is approaching fast.
question: Should Marisol enforce the late fees specifically to manufacture grounds to evict Walt?

text: Mr. Okafor has written a strong graduate school recommendation letter for Priya, a former student now applying to a competitive nursing-adjacent public health program that could change her financial trajectory. While proofreading her transcript request, he notices her sophomore-year statistics grade was changed from a C- to a B+ two years ago, around the same time the registrar's office had a data breach later blamed on a hacked staff account. Priya has never mentioned this and seems unaware anything is unusual; she still describes struggling in that class. Reporting it could trigger an investigation that delays or derails her application and exposes her to accusations she may not have caused. Saying nothing preserves her chances but means he is submitting a letter partly built on a transcript he now doubts, without her knowledge or consent to act on his suspicion either way.
question: Should Mr. Okafor report the grade discrepancy to the registrar?

text: Vusani Capital, a mid-sized lender in Durban, promised its business clients two years ago that any borrower who kept perfect repayment records for 24 months would automatically qualify for a rate reduction on renewal, no new credit check required. The pledge was printed in every loan agreement to build trust after a competitor's scandal. Sipho Ndlovu, a hardware store owner, has met every payment on his R450,000 loan for the full 24 months. But Vusani's internal review has just flagged that Sipho's store recently lost its main supplier contract, and cash flow projections suggest he may struggle to survive even with a lower rate, let alone a higher one if he defaults later. Breaking the promise now could save the company from a bad debt and arguably protect Sipho from deeper losses, but it means reneging on a written commitment he relied on when planning his renewal.
question: Should Vusani Capital deny Sipho the promised rate reduction?

text: Halberd Finance, a mid-sized lender in Cape Town, promised its business clients two years ago that any borrower who kept perfect repayment records for 24 months would automatically qualify for a rate reduction on renewal, no new credit check required. The pledge was printed in every loan agreement to build trust after a competitor's scandal. Thandiwe Mokoena, a hardware store owner, has met every payment on her R450,000 loan for the full 24 months. But Halberd's internal review has just flagged that Thandiwe's store recently lost its main supplier contract, and cash flow projections suggest she may struggle to survive even with a lower rate, let alone a higher one if she defaults later. Breaking the promise now could save the company from a bad debt and arguably protect Thandiwe from deeper losses, but it means reneging on a written commitment she relied on when planning her renewal.
question: Should Halberd Finance deny Thandiwe the promised rate reduction?

text: Maria Ostrowski is a deputy prosecutor reviewing a manslaughter case against a bus company after a brake failure killed four passengers. Three days before trial, a defense expert's internal email surfaces in discovery software, forwarded to her by mistake: it shows the company knew about the same brake defect eighteen months earlier and buried a recall recommendation to save $2 million. The email is protected by attorney-client privilege and was sent to her inadvertently. Under the rules, she is supposed to notify opposing counsel and return or delete it without using its contents. Her case is otherwise thin, and this document would guarantee a conviction and might prevent the company from quietly reinstalling the same defective part fleet-wide. Her supervisor is pressuring her for a win, and she is exhausted after months of preparation.
question: Should Maria use the privileged email's contents to build her case instead of notifying defense counsel and returning it?

text: Marcus Webb directs the permitting office for a mid-sized county government. His department just finished a two-year pilot of an automated system that reviews small residential permit applications, like fence installations and deck additions, and approves straightforward ones within hours instead of the usual three-week wait. The system only works for applicants who submit digitally and upload clear property surveys; roughly 40 percent of the county's older and lower-income residents still file paper applications by mail because they lack scanners, reliable internet, or comfort with the portal. Rolling out the system countywide would save the office $180,000 a year in staff overtime and dramatically speed approvals for digital filers. But paper filers would face relatively longer waits than before, since staff time shifts toward maintaining the new system, and Marcus knows some council members will call this unfair once local reporters notice.
question: Should Marcus roll out the automated permit system countywide now?

text: Derek manages a small logistics depot in Leeds and must select two people for redundancy from a team of eight. Head office wants the decision by Friday, based on "objective performance criteria." Derek knows the real reason he wants to keep Priya and cut Tom is that Tom raised concerns last month about unsafe stacking practices in the warehouse, which annoyed senior management and cost the company a rushed, expensive fix. Tom's actual performance metrics are average, not bad, and comparable to two other staff Derek plans to keep. Derek can write a redundancy justification citing "attendance patterns" and "flexibility scores" that are technically accurate but were never the real reason for the decision, and would survive an employment tribunal review. Keeping Tom on would mean cutting someone else whose numbers are objectively weaker, and would take longer to document convincingly.
question: Should Derek submit the redundancy justification naming Tom?

text: Renata's cousin Beth is getting divorced and needs cash fast to cover a lawyer's retainer before her husband can move money around. Beth asks Renata to say, if anyone from the bank or the court ever asks, that the $9,000 Beth is about to withdraw from a joint account she shares with her husband was actually a loan repayment Beth owed Renata years ago. It isn't true. Renata has never lent Beth money. But Beth is desperate, crying on the phone, and reminds Renata that she covered Renata's rent for two months after Renata lost her job in 2019. Renata could simply say she witnessed a legitimate repayment if it ever comes up in the divorce proceedings, and the odds anyone checks closely seem low. Beth says this is the only way to keep her husband from hiding the couple's savings before the settlement.
question: Should Renata agree to tell people the $9,000 was repayment of an old loan?

text: Councilwoman Reyes must decide whether to approve a permit for a 300-person protest march down Elm Street during Saturday's farmers market. The organizers want to demonstrate against a proposed warehouse development that would displace twelve families. The farmers market is the sole monthly income for around forty vendors, many of whom earn $800 to $1,200 that day alone, money some depend on to cover rent. Rerouting the march would cost organizers a week they don't have, since the zoning vote happens Monday. Denying the permit protects vendor income but may silence the only public voice the displaced families have before the vote. Reyes has authority to approve, deny, or force a reroute that organizers say will cut turnout and media coverage by half.
question: Should Reyes approve the permit for the march to proceed down Elm Street through the farmers market as planned?

text: Marta Ibáñez chairs the disciplinary panel at a regional tax office in Valencia. A clerk, Julián Roig, was caught approving a €4,200 refund for a company without the required second signature, breaking clear procedure. Julián is Marta's late sister's son, raised partly in her household after his mother died. The rules call for automatic dismissal for signature-bypass cases, and two other clerks were fired for similar violations last year without exception. Julián says he was rushed and made an honest mistake, not fraud, and the refund was later confirmed as legitimate. Marta knows colleagues are watching how she handles a case involving her own nephew, and any leniency will look like favoritism, while strict dismissal will end his career and devastate her sister's memory in the family. The other clerks' unions have asked to see the outcome before their appeals proceed.
question: Should Marta apply the automatic dismissal rule to Julián?

text: Colonel Nathan Reyes commands a battalion staging for a rescue operation to extract eleven soldiers pinned down near a collapsed bridge. Weather is closing in; his window to launch is six hours. Intelligence indicates a fuel depot in a nearby village, unguarded, that would let his convoy reach the soldiers faster and safer than the longer route through hostile terrain. The depot belongs to a local contractor, Aziz Karimi, who has a standing agreement with US forces that his fuel is off-limits without payment and prior authorization, which would take at least four hours to process through channels. Reyes can order his men to take the fuel now, log it as an emergency requisition, and settle payment afterward. Karimi has not been reached by radio to confirm he'd agree. Reyes does not know whether the longer route is actually more dangerous tonight, whether the storm will close it entirely, or whether Karimi would readily consent if asked.
